input: The float for the upgrade project currently stands at 10%, and there is a strong case for holding it at that level, which rests essentially on where the remaining uncertainty in the programme actually sits. The steering group has before it a proposal to trim the float, largely on the ground that the design is now settled. It is true that the design is settled in outline; however, the items that actually consume float are not, for the most part, design items at all. They are, rather, the interfaces with the running plant: tie-in windows that depend on operations, deliveries whose dates the project does not control, and ground conditions that only excavation can finally settle. A lower float would effectively price those items as if they were already known quantities. At 10%, by contrast, the programme is able to absorb a slipped tie-in or a late delivery without moving the completion date that the business has planned around; below that figure, the very first slip would move the date, and the resulting cost of the move would fall outside the programme. The figures underpinning this argument are set out in the cost table in the Costs section and are therefore not repeated here. The steering group is accordingly asked to hold the allowance at its present level until the tie-ins have been completed, the long-lead deliveries are on site, and the excavation has revealed what the ground actually contains.
